/world/2026/nov/13/faa-nationwide-ground.headline: FAA reopens US airspace and calls for major air traffic control upgrade
/world/2026/nov/13/faa-nationwide-ground.bodyHtml:
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has reopened the country's airspace and lifted a nationwide ground stop declared on Friday afternoon, after identifying the fault that brought down the US air traffic control system. “So at 8.15 tonight, Eastern Time, we’ve opened up the airspace,” Sean Duffy, the US transportation secretary, said. “But it’s going to take us some time to unwind what’s happened this afternoon.”

Duffy said that the federal government has “identified the problem” that brought down the system on Friday and that it “is operational right now”. The FAA confirmed the airspace was open in an advisory on its website, and said in a statement that it had “thoroughly tested” its systems to confirm they were stable and reliable before clearing flights to resume.

US airlines including United, Delta, Southwest and American Airlines announced they were resuming flights on Friday night after the ground stop was lifted. United said it was restarting operations, “including some Friday night flights”, while American Airlines said it was focused on “operating as many remaining flights as possible this evening”.

The outage had delayed or cancelled more than 11,000 US flights, according to aviation tracker FlightAware, and thrown airports into sudden chaos. Duffy said that more than 3,500 airplanes were in the air when the ground stop was issued; a ground-stop order requires that aircraft remain on the ground and bars them from taking off, though planes already in the air are usually allowed to remain there.

Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, said preliminary investigations into the stoppage did not indicate that it was tied to a “nefarious attack”. “There’s no indication as of yet that this was a nefarious attack against it. It’s just a telecommunications outage as of right now,” he told reporters.

According to CNN, the FAA told airlines that the outages were the result of router malfunctions believed to have originated at Chicago Midway international airport and rippled across the rest of the US. “What we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system,” Duffy said. “Our routers actually got overloaded with data, and … they started to give us inconsistency in the data from those routers. And because of that, we shut the system down,” he added.

The White House briefing on Friday evening with Duffy and Mullin turned into a plea for funding from Congress to “fully fund a full build of a brand new air traffic control system”. Last year, Congress approved $12.5bn to fix the FAA’s ageing communications system, and on Friday the FAA and White House asked Congress for another $30.1bn to address other issues.

Last week, the FAA announced that the first digital air traffic control towers in the US were officially operational in Alaska and Florida, as part of a modernisation project intended to reduce flight delays and improve the flow of air traffic.

Earlier Friday, Duffy had said in a social media post that the stoppage was due to “a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers” and that the FAA’s technicians were looking into the matter. A notice from the FAA said the ground stop was being imposed “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety”.

Amid the uncertainty, San Francisco international airport announced in a social media post that flights bound for Hawaii and Asia were cleared to depart. John F Kennedy airport posted on its social media that travellers should confirm flight status with the airline before heading to the airport.

As news of the airspace reopening trickled down to airline passengers, not all greeted the news with joy. A woman at John F Kennedy airport in New York who gave her name as simply Lola said she was frustrated. She had already rebooked her flight to Atlanta for another day and was going home. “I don’t like it,” she said.

Amid the earlier confusion at US airports, the California governor, Gavin Newsom, called the Trump administration to offer more clarity to passengers who are trying to get to their destinations. “Americans are stuck at airports across the country. They deserve answers, clear updates, and a plan to get home safely. Instead, the Trump Administration is correcting reporters on AI’s “preferred name”. These are not serious people,” Newsom wrote in a post on X, in reference to Mullin correcting a reporter’s use of the term AI earlier in the day.

In an interview on CNN, US congressman Ro Khanna said that he is waiting to be briefed on what exactly led to the technical issues and sparked the ground stoppage and for more public-facing communications from the transportation secretary. “There’s a lot of nervousness,” Khanna said of the feeling among passengers. “We’re waiting to be briefed in Congress about what, exactly, has happened. We just need communication from them. If they were there every hour briefing the American public, it would help and give us a sense of a timeline.”

British Airways cancelled a flight to New York that had been due to take off from Heathrow at 10.30pm on Friday night, and a spokesperson for Manchester airport confirmed three US-bound flights scheduled to leave on Saturday morning – all operated by Virgin Atlantic – were likely to be affected if the issue was not resolved soon.

This is the third time all departing flights have been grounded in the US. The first time was on 9/11; the other was in January 2023, when the FAA paused all domestic departures for less than two hours after a pilot notification system malfunctioned. The FAA has more than 14,000 air traffic controllers who handle the more than 44,000 flights that take off from airports across the US each day, according to FAA data.

/uk-news/2026/nov/13/david-walliams-alle.headline: Specialist officers support new accusers as Met investigates Walliams claims
/uk-news/2026/nov/13/david-walliams-alle.bodyHtml:
The Metropolitan police say accusers who have come forward with new allegations against David Walliams are being supported by specialist officers, as it launched a criminal investigation into alleged non-recent serious sexual offences involving the entertainer, now in his 50s.

Walliams, 55, was separately accused in reports by ITV and the Guardian this week of using his power and celebrity status to prey on young women and teenagers for sex. He has denied any wrongdoing, being a sexual predator or breaking the law.

The Met said the allegations it was investigating were separate to those reported by the Guardian and ITV but, as part of their investigation, detectives were also proactively reviewing that reporting to establish whether there was any evidence of offences.

The new allegations made to police are understood to have come from several people. Some date back to the 2000s and are described by police as “non-recent serious sexual offences involving a man now in his 50s”.

At least some of those who made reports to the police did so this week and had given initial accounts to detectives from the Met’s specialist crime division. Those accounts were enough for the Met to launch a full criminal investigation by detectives specialising in serious and complex sexual offences.

Police said they were keeping the details of the alleged offences, and where and when they are alleged to have occurred, confidential, to minimise the chances of the people who had complained being identified. Detectives stressed that those making the allegations were entitled to life-long anonymity.

It is police policy not to name people under investigation, and in a statement announcing the criminal investigation, the force said: “In recent days, the Met has received a number of allegations of non-recent serious sexual offences involving a man now in his 50s.

“Those who have come forward are being supported by specialist officers.

“The allegations are separate from those reported by ITN and the Guardian. However, as part of their investigation, detectives are also proactively reviewing that reporting to establish whether there is any evidence of offences.”

The Guardian and ITV News reported the allegations against Walliams after a court rejected a legal attempt aimed at preventing publication. Walliams has not been arrested and is in a medical facility.

Det Supt Mike Cagney, from the Met’s complex sexual offences unit which is leading the investigation, said: “We would encourage anyone who has been the victim of a sexual offence to come forward and speak to us, no matter when it happened.

“We know reporting allegations of this nature can be daunting, but specialist officers are on hand to provide support, answer questions and guide you through the process.”

In a letter addressed to journalists working on the media investigation, Walliams wrote: “Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with.

“I realise I did not always take people’s feelings properly into account. That is something I regret. And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did.”

He added: “I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me.”

Police have not carried out any searches as part of their investigation, and say one of their central aims is to support and keep the confidence of those who have complained to them about being victims of sexual offending.

The allegations made to the Guardian include accounts from two women who said they first met Walliams when they were 15 years old. Both women, now in their 30s, said they felt they had been groomed by him two decades ago, and that the experience had continued to affect them.

Walliams was accused of abusing his position to pursue women through the family television show Britain’s Got Talent and at his former children’s book publisher, HarperCollins, where he is alleged to have had a sexual relationship with a junior member of staff.

The allegations were revealed in a joint investigation by the Guardian and ITV News that heard from 30 sources with first-hand accounts of his conduct.

Since the allegations were published, Walliams has been dropped by his literary agency, the BBC has begun to remove his programmes from iPlayer and the Labour party has suspended his membership.

The Met said people could report information to police by calling 101 and providing the reference 4900/10NOV26, or by contacting the complex sexual offences unit on 0207 175 2738.

• Support for anyone affected by sexual abuse issues is available in the UK from Rape Crisis on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland, or 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland. The National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac) offers support for adult survivors on 0808 801 0331. Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. Other international helplines are available for people affected by sexual abuse and childhood abuse, and people in crisis.

/uk-news/2026/nov/13/us-air-force-respon.headline: USAF resolves Lakenheath drone scare without harm
/uk-news/2026/nov/13/us-air-force-respon.bodyHtml:
No personnel, aircraft or infrastructure were affected at RAF Lakenheath, the US Air Force has said, after it responded to “suspected unauthorised drone activity” on Friday night at the Suffolk airbase.

Sirens were heard at the base, one of several in the UK used by the US military.

The USAF said: “We continue to work closely with our host nation counterparts to ensure the safety and security of our US service members, US and host nation civilians, contractors and all of our families.

“Protecting our shared community is a joint responsibility, and we encourage everyone to support this effort by reporting any unusual or suspicious activity to local authorities.”

A UK Ministry of Defence spokesperson said: “We are coordinating with all relevant parties regarding reports of unauthorised drone activity at RAF Lakenheath this evening.

“USAF security forces personnel responded to the reports and the situation is now resolved. We are working closely with them to establish the facts. We will provide updates in due course.”

The MP for West Suffolk, Nick Timothy, said the authorities at the base had told him “there is no threat to the public, and the incident is now resolved”.

Timothy added: “Given the raised threat level, I continue to encourage everyone to report anything suspicious or out of the ordinary to the authorities.”

RAF Lakenheath said in September it was on “Charlie alert”, the second-highest threat level that can be issued by the US department of defense.

It is home to the 48th fighter wing, also known as the Liberty wing, with almost 7,000 active-duty personnel making it the largest US fighter operation in Europe, according to the official base website.

Earlier this year, police investigated an alleged terror plot at RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire and a trespass incident at RAF Molesworth in Cambridgeshire. Both bases are used by the US Air Force.

In the past two months the US has evacuated planes from RAF Mildenhall in Suffolk and RAF Fairford in response to suspected attacks on the bases allegedly linked to Iran.

Donald Trump said in October that “some threats” led the US to pull its bombers from Fairford.

Police said petrol but no explosives were found during searches of vans near the base in Gloucestershire.

Two men were charged by the Crown Prosecution Service over their alleged involvement in the incident.

This week, at least 12 USAF aircraft departed the nearby RAF Mildenhall base including two Boeing Stratotanker KC-135 refuelling aircraft, with one headed towards Germany and another seen landing at Prestwick airport near Glasgow.

Downing Street insisted earlier this week that British airbases are safe and their security is a “top priority”.

/technology/2026/nov/13/microsoft-outage.headline: Microsoft apologises as it gradually restores services after global outage
/technology/2026/nov/13/microsoft-outage.bodyHtml:
Microsoft has said it has “addressed the underlying issue” behind a widespread outage and is “deeply sorry” for the disruption it caused to millions of users, organisations and businesses across the globe.

The company said the outage, a “technical issue” not related to cyber-attacks or AI agents, lasted roughly 18 hours after it began on Thursday evening, with services starting to recover just before midday GMT on Friday; it said it was bringing back services gradually to ensure a stable restoration.

Earlier on Friday, it said email queues were “significantly reduced and approaching normal levels” as it brought back services. More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps, and more than 90% of Fortune 500 companies use Copilot, Microsoft’s AI chatbot, according to the company.

Microsoft has suggested the outage may have been caused by problems with the settings applied to servers responsible for keeping Microsoft 365 up and running.

Mark Gregory, an associate professor in the School of Engineering at RMIT University in Melbourne, said the outage appeared to be affecting the network layer in Microsoft’s systems, and was potentially similar to the configuration issue that brought down Optus’s network in 2023.

He said that when some of the servers had configuration issues, it meant customers were forced to share a smaller pool of servers to access the cloud services.

“If you lose part of that pool, then all of the users are trying to access the remaining servers, and that overloads them. And then they go down. And so you end up with a cascading problem. Then it takes time to find the underlying problem, in this case, a misconfiguration in the network layer.”

Gregory said businesses reliant on cloud services such as Microsoft 365 should have backup options.

Microsoft’s executive vice-president of Copilot, Charles Lamanna, said: “We regret that today’s outages caused disruptions for our customers, and we are working to address the issue.”

On Friday, government agencies worldwide, from municipalities in France to the US House of Representatives, reported problems with Microsoft services. The issues were patchy, with some but not all users reporting problems with services including Microsoft Teams and Outlook email.

The outage website Down Detector showed an increase in Microsoft 365 problems at about 6pm GMT on Thursday, with nearly 130,000 reports of problems in 74 countries affecting access to Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook and Teams as well as enterprise services such as SharePoint and OneDrive. Copilot was also affected.

The Microsoft outage also hit connectors used by OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s AI services.

OpenAI said it was investigating a problem with Microsoft connectors in which new connections might be broken and tools were not working as expected. Anthropic said it had identified an issue with an upstream provider affecting its Microsoft 365 connector.

The outage has affected businesses and organisations across the world that use Microsoft products.

In the UK, healthcare systems were disrupted and several British police forces urged people not to try to report crimes online and to phone them in instead.

Some schools in the UK notified parents that reporting attendance or absence issues had to be done via phone. National Rail, which provides information across the UK network, warned people might not be able to access tickets that had been emailed to them.

US government offices across the country have been affected by the outage, including congressional offices that heavily rely on Outlook email. The US House’s chief administrative officer that handles IT for the chamber sent out a “campus-wide alert” to staffers on Thursday about the outage, Politico reported.

Multiple cities, including the City of Tampa, Florida, posted notices on their municipal websites to say that they were affected by the outage. Law enforcement offices across the US were also affected, with one sheriff’s county in Colorado saying it was unable to process bond payments because Outlook email was down, and requesting that anyone who needed to post bond do so in person.

When stock market trading opened on Wall Street, shares in Microsoft dipped slightly, down 1.1% at $516.86.

In Australia, the financial impact of the outage was expected to cost billions of dollars, according to the risk advisory firm, RSM Australia. Several government agencies, including national security sevices, were unable to access or send emails.

Hospitals and health clinics were affected, although the Australian Medical Association on Friday said had been no impacts for patient care. Courts and schools also struggled to operate as normal.

The Indian airlines IndiGo and Akasa Air said their email support services were affected, and Taiwanese security firms, life insurers and investment trust companies said fund management services had been disrupted.

In financial markets some portfolio managers have been unable to check emails, making it hard to access on some trading platforms.

In Japan, the shipping company Sagawa Express said it was unable to accept online reservations for some of its services at airports and train stations while Taisho, a leading pharmaceutical company, said it was having to handle orders by phone.

Microsoft last month reported an outage of its Azure cloud platform that affected a suite of productivity software and a range of industries worldwide.

Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report

/politics/2026/nov/13/nigel-farage-perso.headline: Labour and Tories demand Farage explain Reform UK's funding of his security
/politics/2026/nov/13/nigel-farage-perso.bodyHtml:
Labour and the Conservatives have demanded that Nigel Farage give a full account of how he has spent an undisclosed £5m gift from a billionaire donor, after sources told the Guardian his personal security has in fact been paid for out of Reform UK's central funds instead.

The Reform leader has had the central party pay for a team and two cars ever since a reduction in the security provided by the taxpayer after a review in 2025.

The disclosure raises fresh questions about Farage’s explanation of the £5m he was given by the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne.

Bridget Phillipson, the Labour party chair, said: “Nigel Farage’s excuses over his secret £5m ‘gift’ have fallen apart. You can’t trust a word he says. From secret gifts, to police investigations into Reform’s finances, to donations from a convicted fraudster – Reform are up to their necks in sleaze and scandal. Farage and his party are simply not fit for office. It’s time for him to get his story straight and be honest with the public.”

A Conservative party spokesperson said: “Nigel Farage variously described his fishy bung from an overseas crypto billionaire as a reward for Brexit, cash he can spend on Ferraris or the horses if he wants, the list goes on. It is no wonder people are asking questions, and the public are entitled to a straight answer. Nigel Farage should come clean about where the £5m has gone and what it was really for.”

After the Guardian revealed the gift, Harborne said it was intended “to support Nigel’s security not just now but for the rest of his life”.

Farage initially said: “This money was given to me so that I would be safe and secure for the rest of my life.”

He suggested that the Home Office did not offer him any security support. In fact, though it was reduced in scale, he was offered a bodyguard, a driver and car – similar to the provision made for Kemi Badenoch, the leader of the official opposition.

Farage refused this, and since then his security has been paid for from central party funds. These costs have amounted to more than £150,000 in the past year, sources said.

The arrangement has caused consternation for some within the party. “It’s completely at odds with the narrative he’s tried to sell the public,” a Reform source said.

Asked about Farage expensing the party, a spokesperson for Reform UK said: “As a standard practice, we do not comment on security matters.”

The party refused to answer questions about whether Farage had spent any of the £5m on security costs to date. It also refused to address questions about why Farage had refused the offer of a taxpayer-funded package.

The Guardian understands that the party makes a distinction between security required as a result of its leader’s political activities, which it pays for, and his potential longer-term personal security needs, which the gift was intended to provide for.

Zia Yusuf, Reform’s spokesperson for home affairs, complained publicly that the party was having to seek fresh support from donors to meet Farage’s security costs in October 2025.

Harborne gave Farage £5m shortly before he stood as an MP in the 2024 general election. On becoming an MP, Farage was offered and accepted taxpayer-funded security, which he used until autumn 2025.

Harborne had been the dominant party donor in recent years until he was joined by his fellow crypto tycoon Ben Delo in donating a further £36m each in September.

Costs charged to Reform by Farage have included security changes to his properties, including ones used by his family members, according to sources.

The security team funded by Reform has also been used by Farage for personal activities, sources said.

Since Harborne’s initial claim that the gift was intended to fund his security arrangements, Farage’s account of what the £5m gift was for has varied. He has said he could spend it on Ferraris, or that it was a reward for Brexit campaigning, and at other times he has tried to suggest it was not political but for his security for life.

Footage gathered by the undercover reporting group Verbatim and shared with the Guardian last month appeared to show that Farage’s close aide Dan Jukes believed it was a PR mistake for Farage to suggest it was for anything other than security.

“That was not the line to take from the press office,” Jukes said, after Farage suggested in an interview with the Sun that the money was a reward for his political campaigning.

Jukes has since stood down from Reform and he denies any wrongdoing.

Lawyers for Harborne have previously said he “expected nothing in return” for the money and “did not envisage Mr Farage returning to politics”.

The timeline for the gift is disputed. Lawyers for Harborne have said the gift was made on 5 April 2024. According to financial industry sources, some of the £5m was not received until the end of May, just before Farage announced on 3 June that he would stand as an MP.

The Guardian has also reported that Farage told senior Reform figures he would need “a million a year” to cover lost earnings if he stood for parliament in 2024.

/society/2026/nov/13/probation-officers-.headline: Ministry of Justice presses on with £700m plan to recruit 1,300 probation officers
/society/2026/nov/13/probation-officers-.bodyHtml:
The Ministry of Justice is pressing ahead with a £700m investment package running through 2028-29, which includes recruiting 1,300 more trainee probation officers for the 2026-27 financial year, as it tries to ease the pressure behind a vote by probation staff across England and Wales to strike over pay and workloads.

An MoJ spokesperson said: “Probation staff do a vital job protecting the public, which is why we have put a strong offer on the table, giving every worker a further 5% pay rise, which follows the biggest probation pay increase in over a decade alongside record investment.

“We’re also recruiting an additional 1,300 officers to significantly cut workloads.

“While we are disappointed that some have voted against this competitive deal, it will not change our first responsibility of protecting the public and we have robust contingency plans in place to ensure offenders are still subject to the same rigorous supervision.”

The government’s plans to release thousands of prisoners early were nonetheless dealt a blow on Friday, after members of the union, Napo, backed overtime restrictions and other forms of action short of a strike, which is likely to start on 23 November. Plans are being made for strike action to follow at a later stage.

The union, whose members work across probation offices and in family courts, said it launched its ballot because of an “inadequate” 5% pay offer from ministers and a failure to cut workloads.

Probation officers have come under increasing pressure since the launch of the latest early release scheme in October, which is meant to ease overcrowding in prisons.

They are responsible for monitoring offenders’ behaviour, overseeing their rehabilitation, monitoring their electronic tags and recalling them to prison for any offences or licence breaches, such as entering an exclusion or restriction zone protecting victims.

By the end of the year, about 2,500 offenders, including sex offenders, domestic abusers and stalkers, will be released under the scheme.

The union had sought a 12% increase. Napo general secretary Ian Lawrence said: “The high turnout by our members and the result vindicates the campaign to achieve a pay rise to make up lost ground in comparative pay with other staff employed within HMPPS [HM Prison and Probation Service].

“The vote also reflects serious anger at the state of probation workloads, which were already in crisis before the latest version of the prisoner early release scheme.”

Napo said probation wages have “stagnated” since 2010, with reception staff on a salary just above the minimum wage – the lowest in the civil service.

On pay, Napo members voted by 85% in favour of action short of strike action and 74% in favour of strike action. In a ballot on workloads, the vote was 87% in favour of action short of strike action and 75% in favour of strikes.

The Institute for Government, a thinktank, said slow progress on recruitment means probation practitioners were still overstretched and ill-equipped to absorb additional demand.

It said there had been a serious staff shortage in probation for several years, with the number of probation officers consistently 25-30% below target staffing. As of March 2026, nine probation delivery units (8% of the total) had a vacancy rate of 40% or more.

/world/2026/nov/14/ukraine-war-briefing-.headline: Kallas: EU will not be drawn into Russia's security traps
/world/2026/nov/14/ukraine-war-briefing-.bodyHtml:
• The EU's foreign policy chief warned against “walking into the traps that Russia is setting” as she said Moscow was trying to start a debate about European security in order to divert attention from its aggression, reports Jennifer Rankin. “We have one aggressor and one victim, and the aggressor does not have security concerns,” Kaja Kallas said on arrival at an EU leaders’ summit in Dublin. In talks on the Ukraine war, Russia has revived its hardline demands for a total overhaul of European security – demands that were rejected in 2021.

  • Volodymyr Zelenskyy pressed Ukraine's defence and foreign ministries, together with relevant US bodies, to restore full speed on the Starshield satellite system, saying speed restrictions remain in place on the system, hampering the Ukrainian military’s ability to operate inside the country. The continued restrictions made it hard to intercept jet-powered and other drones and sent a bad signal to Russia on dealing with land seized by Russian forces in the war, the Ukrainian president also said on Friday. “Unfortunately, the speed restrictions remain in place along the entire front line and in temporarily-occupied territories of Ukraine,” he said in his nightly video address. “I expect the ministry of defence and the foreign ministry, together with all relevant structures in the United States, will work through this issue.” Ukrainian officials said in mid-October that Elon Musk’s SpaceX had abruptly capped the speed of Starlink and its Starshield military version amid tensions with the US over Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries. Service was restored on 24 October.

  • Zelenskyy said on Thursday Ukrainian military units had recorded disruptions to Starshield over several days. He repeated that the restrictions “limit our ability to intercept jet-powered Shaheds [Iranian-designed drones] and counter other drones”. “They also send Russia a signal that America may somehow treat our temporarily-occupied land differently,” he said. “We expect the speed to be restored.”

  • Russia attacked a hospital in the centre of Kyiv, close to several western embassies, after Zelenskyy’s comments on the throttling of Starshield. Three people were injured when a drone smashed into the National Institute of Traumatology and Orthopedics at 3am, hitting the second floor of the hospital and an adjoining 19th-century building in the capital, reports Luke Harding. Meanwhile, Russia claimed to have shot down nearly 1,200 Ukrainian drones overnight, one of the largest swarms sent by Kyiv. It said at least four people were killed in the southern region of Volgograd.

  • A general in Ukraine’s SBU security service suspected in a serious corruption case was released from pre-trial detention on Friday after posting $1.2m bail. Footage on Ukraine’s TSN.ua news site showed Serhiy Duka after leaving prison proclaiming his innocence and thanking his SBU “brothers-in-arms” who had raised the bail money. Duka was detained on 4 November as part of an anti-corruption operation targeting an alleged criminal group that investigators say involved members of the SBU, the prosecutor’s office, the police and organised crime.

  • Russia has been rocked by two car bomb attacks that killed a senior military figure and seriously injured a suspected intelligence agent, in the latest in a series of assassination attempts believed to have been orchestrated by Kyiv. On Friday morning a car bomb exploded in southern Moscow, severely injuring Sergei Zavorotniy, 72, a former senior aide to Ukraine’s exiled former prime minister Mykola Azarov, reports Pjotr Sauer. The blast came a day after a car bomb explosion in St Petersburg killed a senior Russian military official. The official has not been publicly identified but a local broadcaster cited sources as saying the victim was a colonel in the Russian air force.

  • Russian forces launched strikes on two Ukrainian cities on Friday, killing one person and injuring more than 50 in the south-eastern city of Zaporizhzhia and killing two more in the Black Sea port of Odesa, regional officials said. In Zaporizhzhia, a five-storey apartment building was hit and seriously damaged. A rescue worker was killed when a concrete slab collapsed during operations to clear rubble, regional governor Mykhailo Semikin said. In Odesa, two people died in an attack on a private residence, said the city’s military administration head, Serhiy Lysak. Five people were injured.

/film/2026/nov/13/robert-pattinson-repor.headline: Favourable contract terms put Pattinson in pole position for Bond
/film/2026/nov/13/robert-pattinson-repor.bodyHtml:
Robert Pattinson has emerged as the favourite to succeed Daniel Craig as James Bond, according to a credible film-industry source.

Writing in Puck, Matthew Belloni suggests that the favourable contract terms he says have been offered to Pattinson point to the actor, currently in cinemas with reality-crime thriller Primetime, being studio Amazon MGM’s preferred choice for the role.

According to Belloni, while other actors on the shortlist were required to commit to four Bond films, Pattinson’s contract called for three – and offered a much larger (unspecified) fee.

According to Belloni, “it suggests the studio is willing or even eager to sacrifice a bit to get a ‘name’ star to front its most important franchise”.

Producers have run the casting process for the new Bond film, the 26th in the official series, very publicly in recent weeks, with industry reports suggesting that three actors – Callum Turner, Jack Lowden and Josh O’Connor – were on the producers’ shortlist, and two weeks later that two others, Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult, were also being tested.

Each contender will have been offered terms before the test process began – what Belloni calls “test deals” – and Belloni suggests producers brought in more established names because they were not fully satisfied with the original three-strong shortlist.

Bond 26 will be the first film made by the series’ new owner, Amazon MGM, which has “creative control” of the franchise after striking a deal with its previous producers, Eon, in 2025.

Producers David Heyman and Amy Pascal are overseeing the project, while Dune’s Denis Villeneuve will direct and Peaky Blinders’ Steven Knight is writing the script.

Having starred in franchises including Twilight, Harry Potter, The Batman and Dune, and in acclaimed dramas such as Bel Ami, Cosmopolis, The Lost City of Z and The Lighthouse, Pattinson is the most high-profile of the contenders – something that would have likely counted against him when Eon was still in control, whose credo was that Bond was a bigger star than any actor.

Belloni suggests that in the current media landscape, that may no longer hold: “No franchise is bulletproof any more – everything is vulnerable and most can be helped by a value-add element, like an established star.”
